'''John Albert Katzenellenbogen''' (born May 10, 1944) is an American Professor of Chemistry at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign|University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]]. He studies the development of novel agents for the treatment of hormone-responsive and non-responsive [[Breast cancer|breast]] and [[prostate cancer]]s and the design of [[estrogen]]s and [[antiestrogen]]s that have a favorable balance of beneficial versus detrimental effects.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://chemistry.illinois.edu/directory/profile/jkatzene |title=John Katzenellenbogen |publisher=illinois.edu |access-date=December 5, 2017}}</ref>

== Early life ==
John Katzenellenbogen was born May 10, 1944, in [[Poughkeepsie, New York]]. His parents taught at [[Vassar College]], his father a professor of art history and his mother a pianist. His grandfather [[Albert Katzenellenbogen]] was a lawyer in Frankfurt, Germany who died in the Holocaust. In 1958, his family moved to [[Baltimore|Baltimore, Maryland]], where his father [[Adolf Katzenellenbogen]] became Head of the Department of Art History at [[Johns Hopkins University]]<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/10/01/dr-adolf-katzenellenbogen-johns-hopkins-professor-dies.html|title=Dr. Adolf Katzenellenbogen, Johns Hopkins Professor, Dies|date=1964-10-01|work=The New York Times|access-date=2017-11-23|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> and his mother joined the faculty at [[Peabody Institute|Peabody Conservatory]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sfcm.edu/faculty/scott-foglesong|title=Scott Foglesong {{!}} SFCM|website=sfcm.edu|access-date=2017-11-23}}</ref> and [[Goucher College]].<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1970|title=Members of the Society|jstor=40376030|journal=College Music Symposium|volume=10|pages=182}}</ref> He began playing the cello at age 10. Katzenellenbogen attended [[Gilman School]]<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://issuu.com/gilmancommunications/docs/56594_gilmanfinal/64|title=Fall 2015 Gilman Bulletin|work=issuu|access-date=2017-11-23|language=en}}</ref> and held various summer jobs: in 1960, he worked at the Research Institute for Advanced Studies in the photosynthesis lab of Dr. Bessel Kok,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.hcs.harvard.edu/coreylab/notes/notes.php|title=Notes: Elias James Corey|website=www.hcs.harvard.edu|access-date=2017-11-23}}</ref> and, in 1961, he was a General Electric Student Research Fellow at [[Union College]] in [[Schenectady, New York]]. As an undergraduate at [[Harvard University|Harvard]], he majored in chemistry, going on to complete a PhD in chemistry in 1969 at Harvard under the direction of [[Elias James Corey|Dr. E. J. Corey]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.hcs.harvard.edu/coreylab/members/members.php|title=Group Members: Elias James Corey|website=www.hcs.harvard.edu|access-date=2017-11-23|archive-date=2021-04-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210422125331/http://www.hcs.harvard.edu/coreylab/members/members.php|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Career ==
Katzenellenbogen began his academic career as an Assistant Professor of Chemistry at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://chemistry.illinois.edu/directory/profile/jkatzene|title=John A. Katzenellenbogen {{!}} Chemistry at Illinois|website=chemistry.illinois.edu|language=en|access-date=2017-11-22}}</ref> in 1969 and was promoted to Associate Professor in 1975 and to Full Professor in 1979. He was named the Roger Adams Professor and subsequently the chaired Swanlund Professor of Chemistry. He was one of the first academic chemists to work in the field of [[chemical biology]]. His major research efforts have focused on the study of steroid hormones and their biological receptors, the [[estrogen receptor]] in particular.

Katzenellenbogen's research is highly collaborative, and he works with other scientists locally, nationally, and internationally. He has published more than 550 articles<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Katzenellenbogen+JA|title=Katzenellenbogen JA – PubMed – NCBI|last=pubmeddev|website=www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov|access-date=2017-11-22}}</ref> and has trained over 130 PhD's and Postdoctoral Associates. He is a member of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] and a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], on whose National Council he served for many years. He has received numerous awards from scientific societies, including the Arthur C. Cope Scholar Award,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/arthur-cope-scholar-award.html|title=Arthur C. Cope Scholar Awards – American Chemical Society|website=American Chemical Society|language=en|access-date=2017-11-22}}</ref> the E. B. Hershberg Award for Important Discoveries in Medicinally Active Substances from the [[American Chemical Society]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/e-b-hershberg-award-for-important-discoveries-in-medicinally-active-substances.html|title=E. B. Hershberg Award for Important Discoveries in Medicinally Active Substances – American Chemical Society|website=American Chemical Society|language=en|access-date=2017-11-22}}</ref> the Endocrine Society's Fred Conrad Koch Lifetime Achievement Award,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://chemistry.illinois.edu/news/2015-09-01/katzenellenbogens-awarded-fred-conrad-koch-lifetime-achievement-award-endocrine|title=Katzenellenbogens Awarded Fred Conrad Koch Lifetime Achievement Award by the Endocrine Society {{!}} Chemistry at Illinois|website=chemistry.illinois.edu|language=en|access-date=2017-11-22}}</ref> which he shared with [[Benita Katzenellenbogen|Dr. Benita Katzenellenbogen]], and the Award for Outstanding Achievements in Chemistry in Cancer Research from the [[American Association for Cancer Research]] In 2018, Katzenellenbogen was inducted into the [[Medicinal chemistry|Medicinal Chemistry]] Hall of Fame of the American Chemical Society.
